title: Which of these seven sets of lengths make a triangle?
description: Seven sets of lengths are tested one by one by comparing the longest length with the other two added together. Three sets fail the check and four pass.
teaching_notes: One idea: for each set, compare the longest length with the other two added together. Watch for children who compare the two shorter lengths with each other, or who accept a set when the two sides are equal.

source: Which of the following lengths can be the sidelengths of a triangle? Explain your answers. Note that for each set, the three lengths have the same unit of measure. (a) 2, 2, 5 (b) 3, 4, 6 (c) 2, 4, 8 (d) 5, 5, 8 (e) 10, 20, 25 (f) 10, 20, 35 (g) 24, 26, 28
video_script.why: The child has seen that the longest side decides the matter and now applies the comparison to seven sets in a row.
video_script.substitution: In each set the longest length is compared with the other two added together, in that set's own unit.
video_script.anchor: Seven sets of three lengths, in a list from the first set to the seventh set
video_script.payoff_line: Triangles exist for the second, fourth, fifth and seventh sets.

final_answer.value: Triangles exist for (b) 3, 4, 6; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (g) 24, 26, 28. Not for (a), (c) or (f)
final_answer.spoken: triangles exist for the second, fourth, fifth and seventh sets, and not for the first, third and sixth sets

never_show: the words triangles exist before the answer beat
maths_rules: arcs for (a) would leave a gap of 5 - 4 = 1
video_script.design: One idea: compare the longest length with the other two added together. The seven sets stay in the anchor band; the working band holds the board solution.

beats.on_screen: seven cards labelled a to g with three lengths each; a question mark
narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book.
Seven sets of three lengths are given, and each set has one unit.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which sets can be the sides of a triangle?

beats.on_screen: the seven cards and the question mark stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a rough triangle with its longest side in red and the other two sides in yellow

marks.compare: the longest side and the other two sides are marked

beats.colours: longest in red, the other two in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Use the same way as the last two videos.
<bookmark mark='compare'/>Compare the longest length with the other two added together.

marks.given: the seven sets are written in a list

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the seven sets, in the order of the book.

beats.on_screen: To find: which sets pass the check?
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which sets pass the check.
<bookmark mark='a'/>Step one, the first set has the longest length five.
Two plus two is four, which is less than five.
This set fails the check.

beats.colours: tick in green, cross in red
narration: <bookmark mark='b'/>Step two, in the second set three plus four is seven.
Seven is more than six, so it passes.
<bookmark mark='c'/>In the third set two plus four is six.
Six is less than eight, so it fails.
<bookmark mark='d'/>Step three, in the fourth set five plus five is ten.
Ten is more than eight, so it passes.
<bookmark mark='e'/>In the fifth set ten plus twenty is thirty.
Thirty is more than twenty five, so it passes.

beats.colours: tick in green, cross in red
narration: <bookmark mark='f'/>Step four, in the sixth set ten plus twenty is thirty.
Thirty is less than thirty five, so it fails.
<bookmark mark='g'/>In the seventh set twenty four plus twenty six is fifty.
Fifty is more than twenty eight, so it passes.

beats.on_screen: Step 5: check (a): arcs of 2 and 2 on a base of 5 leave a gap of 1

marks.check: a base of 5 with two arcs of 2 is drawn
marks.gap: a gap of 1 glows between the arcs

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step five, check the first set with arcs.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>Two arcs of two on a base of five leave a gap of one.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Triangles exist for (b) 3, 4, 6; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (g) 24, 26, 28. Not for (a), (c) or (f)
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Triangles exist for the second, fourth, fifth and seventh sets.
They do not exist for the first, third and sixth sets.
